headline: Thailand's Leopard Cat Rescue Center Prepares Orphaned Cubs for Wild Life
meta_description: A government wildlife center in northeastern Thailand rehabilitates dozens of orphaned leopard cat cubs yearly, teaching them survival skills before release in…
summary_short: A Thai wildlife rescue center trains orphaned leopard cats to hunt and climb before releasing them into the wild, improving survival rates through specialized care.
body:
At a government-run wildlife rescue center in Khon Kaen, northeastern Thailand, orphaned leopard cat cubs learn to be wild. The center rehabilitates and releases dozens of these small felines each year, many rescued from agricultural fires or found injured by farmers. Since 2023, admissions have jumped dramatically—from an annual average of around 10 cubs to between 40 and 65 yearly—driven by worsening habitat fragmentation, increased fire activity, and greater public awareness through a government hotline. Staff report that this year alone, more than 60 cubs arrived from across the region, with over half found in charred fields bearing burn injuries. The center has achieved significant progress: while 20 of this year's 60 admissions did not survive, this represents a notably lower mortality rate of 33 percent compared to 60 percent in previous years.

The rehabilitation process is meticulous. Young cubs arriving at the center receive formula milk feedings multiple times daily before transitioning to solid food. Once weaned, they enter specialized behavioral pens—each measuring around 24 square meters and housing two cats—where vegetation, tree trunks, and dark nooks recreate a natural habitat. Here, the cats practice climbing and hunting skills lost when separated from their mothers at a young age. Staff introduce live chicks and mice to stimulate the cats' predatory instincts, preparing them for independent survival. Before release, each cat receives a full health examination, microchip implant, and disease screening to prevent introducing infections into wild populations.

While the center can monitor released cats through camera traps, staff acknowledge they currently have no way to confirm how many animals survive after leaving captivity. Still, the program represents a crucial lifeline for a species increasingly threatened by habitat loss and human activity. These small wild felines, no larger than a human hand when rescued, are being given a second chance at the life they were meant to live.
quick_facts: Thailand's Khon Kaen rescue center admits 40-65 leopard cat cubs yearly, up from 10 before 2023
Mortality rate improved to 33% this year, down from 60% in previous years
Over half of 60 cubs admitted in 2026 were found in charred agricultural fields
Rehabilitation pens measure 24 square meters, housing two cats with live prey for hunting practice
Veterinarians microchip and screen all cats for diseases before release into the wild
